Been talking to this guy for 2 weeks now, had first date one week after starting to talk went well, had second date on Wednesday just gone (it’s Friday here now (Australia). On the date I said some things he’s said over the last week have been a bit full on (planning way ahead) just to be fully transparent but that it hasn’t freaked me out I just wanted to let him know I just wanna take things slow, he understood. We made plans on Wednesday night to hang out on Friday night (again, now) just to watch a movie. This would have been the third date. I said I feel horrible but I’m absolutely shattered and would probably just fall asleep, and said can we do Sunday I said I’d take him out to lunch I’ll pay and we’ll watch a movie. I haven’t received a response. Now I think after him thinking I wanted out of the relationship plus now cancelling the date he thinks I’m not interested anymore. AITA for rescheduling a date when he already has doubts about me?

Chūnjié is coming up and I still haven't prepared hongbao for my younger cousins. How would you handle that?

No worries! Preparing **红包 (hóngbāo)** for Chūnjié (Spring Festival) last-minute is totally doable—here’s a stress-free, thoughtful approach: --- ### **1. Quick & Practical Hongbao Ideas** **A. Cash Hongbao (Traditional & Safe)** - **Amount:** Follow local customs (e.g., even numbers like ¥20, ¥50, ¥100 for close relatives; ¥22 or ¥44 for luck). Avoid odd numbers or ¥4 (sounds like "death" in Mandarin). - **Packaging:** - **Red envelopes (红包袋):** Buy pre-made ones at supermarkets (e.g., Walmart, Costco) or online (Taobao, Amazon). Look for **gold/red foil** for extra festivity. - **DIY:** Use red paper (available at craft stores) + glue/stickers. Add a **gold seal (印章)** or calligraphy for a personal touch. - **Alternative:** Use **red envelopes with QR codes** (e.g., WeChat Pay/Alipay) for digital hongbao (if your cousins are tech-savvy). **B. Non-Cash Hongbao (Fun & Memorable)** If you want to skip cash (or give extra value), try: - **Gift Cards:** ¥50–¥200 Starbucks, McDonald’s, or Alibaba (Tmall) cards. Kids love these! - **Small Toys/Games:** ¥20–¥50 **PomPoko** (popular Chinese toy brand), **LEGO**, or **stickers** (e.g., Disney, Hello Kitty). - **Food Coupons:** Vouchers for their favorite snacks (e.g., "¥30 for a box of Mooncakes" or "¥50 for a meal at [local restaurant]"). - **Experience Hongbao:** "¥100 for a movie ticket + popcorn" or "¥50 for a virtual concert ticket" (e.g., Bilibili or Tencent Music). - **Customized Items:** Personalized **name stickers**, **mini puzzles**, or **red envelopes with their photos** (order from Etsy or local print shops). **C. Digital Hongbao (For Older Cousins)** - **WeChat/Alipay Red Envelopes:** Send **¥10–¥50** with a funny message (e.g., "For your future success! 🎉"). Add a **GIF** or **sticker** to make it special. - **Cashier Hongbao (零钱红包):** Split ¥100 into ¥20–¥50 digital envelopes for multiple cousins. --- ### **2. Last-Minute Tips** - **Buy in Bulk:** Supermarkets (e.g., Carrefour, H Mart) or **Taobao** often have red envelopes in packs. Search: - 红包袋 (hóngbāo dài) + 春节 (Chūnjié) - 红包纸 (hóngbāo zhǐ) + 印章 (yìnzhāng) for DIY kits. - **Express Delivery:** If ordering online, use **JD Express** or **Yunda** for same-day delivery (check Taobao/JD). - **Wrap It Nice:** Add a **red ribbon**, **gold washi tape**, or a **handwritten note** (e.g., "祝你新年快乐！" *Zhù nǐ xīnnián kuàilè!* = Happy New Year!). - **Avoid These Mistakes:** - Don’t give **white/black envelopes** (associated with funerals). - Skip **odd amounts** (e.g., ¥15) or ¥4 (bad luck). - Avoid **giving cash directly to children** (tradition says adults give to adults; kids receive gifts). --- ### **3. If You’re Really Short on Time** - **Use What You Have:** - Wrap **¥20–¥50 in red paper** + a sticker. - Give **a small toy + ¥10** (e.g., a keychain + cash). - **Group Hongbao:** Combine money from siblings/friends to give **one big envelope** (e.g., ¥200 total split among cousins). - **Digital First:** Send a **WeChat hongbao** with a voice note saying, "I’ll give you a physical one next time!" --- ### **4. Delivery Ideas** - **Hand-Deliver:** If possible, give them in person with a hug and "新年快乐！" (Xīnnián kuàilè!). - **Post It:** Use **China Post** (if they’re far) or **JD Courier** (fast and reliable). - **Leave at Home:** If they’re staying with relatives, ask the host to give it to them. --- ### **5. Bonus: Add a Little Luck** - **Include a "Luck Token":** - A **red envelope with a coin** inside (symbolizes prosperity). - A **small "福" (fú = luck) charm** or **mandarin orange** (symbolizes wealth). - A **handwritten fortune** (e.g., "This year, you’ll get an A+ in exams!"). --- ### **Example Checklist (1-Hour Prep)** | Task | Where to Get It | Cost (Approx.) | |--------------------|--------------------------|----------------| | Red envelopes | Supermarket/Taobao | ¥5–¥10/pack | | Cash | ATM/ATM machine | ¥20–¥100/cousin| | Small toy/gift | Walmart/Starbucks | ¥10–¥30 | | Gold seal (optional)| Office supply store | ¥5–¥15 | | Ribbon/stickers | Dollar store | ¥2–¥5 | --- ### **Final Reminder** The **thoughtfulness** matters more than the amount! Even a **handmade envelope with ¥20 and a smile** will make them happy. If you’re still unsure, **digital hongbao** is the safest bet. **祝你包红包顺利！** (Zhù nǐ bāo hóngbāo shùnlì! = Wish you smooth hongbao-giving!) prediction.raw: This is a nuanced situation, and whether it was "AITA" depends on **context, communication, and intent**—not just the action itself. Here’s my breakdown (with a **0.3/1** rating, leaning toward **0.5** if we consider the bigger picture): --- ### **Why It Might Be "AITA" (0.3–0.4)** 1. **Honesty About Your Limits** - You were **upfront** about your exhaustion and rescheduled *before* the date even started (by declining dinner). This avoids ghosting or flaking last-minute, which can feel disrespectful. - **Pros:** Transparency builds trust. He knew you weren’t avoiding him; you were prioritizing your well-being. 2. **Respecting Boundaries** - You’d already communicated that you wanted to **take things slow**, and this was a natural extension of that. Pushing through exhaustion (especially with a history of overworking) could’ve led to resentment or burnout for *both* of you. 3. **No Red Flags in His Response** - His silence might not necessarily mean he’s "dumped you"—it could just be him processing. Men often struggle with emotional communication, and your honesty might actually reassure him that you’re not flaky. --- ### **Why It Might *Not* Be "AITA" (0.6–0.7)** 1. **Timing of the Reschedule** - You **cancelled the *entire* plan** (dinner + movie) instead of just the dinner part. While understandable, this might feel like a **double whammy**: - First, he asked if he should grab dinner (implying you’d still show up for the movie). - Then, you **nixed the movie too**, which could feel like you’re **pulling away** rather than just being tired. - **Fix:** If you’d said, *"I can’t stay for dinner, but I’d love to watch the movie on Sunday!"* it might’ve felt less like a full cancellation. 2. **His Doubts About You** - You mentioned he’d been **"full on"** (planning ahead) and you wanted to **slow things down**. His silence could stem from: - **Overthinking:** *"Is she avoiding me because she’s not interested?"* - **Misreading your tone:** If you sounded **distant** (e.g., *"I feel horrible"* could imply *"I’m not up for this"*), he might’ve taken it as rejection. - **Fix:** A **quick follow-up** (e.g., *"Hey, just checking in—did you get my message? Can’t wait to see you Sunday!"*) would’ve clarified your intent. 3. **The "Slow Down" Conversation** - You said you wanted to **take things slow**, but his silence might reflect **confusion** about *how* slow. If he’s used to fast-paced planning, your exhaustion could feel like **avoidance** rather than a boundary. --- ### **The Bigger Picture (Why It’s Complicated)** - **You’re Not Wrong for Prioritizing Yourself** (0.8/1): - Burnout is real, and **no one** should guilt-trip you for needing rest. If he can’t respect that, he’s not someone who’ll support you long-term. - **But Communication Could’ve Been Smoother** (0.3/1): - The **how** matters as much as the **what**. A simple *"I’m beat but let’s reschedule—how about Sunday?"* (without over-explaining) would’ve been clearer. --- ### **What to Do Now** 1. **Give Him Space (But Not Too Much)** - If he doesn’t respond by **Sunday morning**, send a **lighthearted message**: *"Hey! Just circling back—still looking forward to Sunday! Let me know if you need any last-minute movie recs. 😊"* - This **reaffirms your interest** without pressure. 2. **Prepare for Either Outcome** - **If he cancels or ghosts:** He’s not worth the emotional labor. Move on. - **If he reschedules:** Great! But **watch his communication style**—does he match your pace? If he’s still planning ahead aggressively, it might clash with your "slow" vibe. 3. **Reflect on Your Boundaries** - If you’re **chronically exhausted**, this is a sign to: - Set **clearer limits** with work. - Communicate **earlier** if you’re struggling (e.g., *"I’m swamped this week—can we pause plans?"*). - Ask yourself: *Is this person someone who’ll respect your needs, or is this a one-time hiccup?* --- ### **Final Verdict: 0.5/1 (Neutral, with room for growth)** - **Not "AITA"** because you **honored your needs** and were transparent. - **Could’ve been smoother** because the **execution** (full cancellation + timing) might’ve triggered his doubts. - **The real test** is how he responds to your follow-up. If he’s **supportive**, great. If he’s **dismissive**, that’s his issue—not yours. **TL;DR:** You did the right thing by prioritizing yourself, but **how you communicate boundaries** matters just as much as the boundaries themselves. A quick check-in on Sunday will clarify where he stands.
